context: Trap #1 — The “17-Dot Head Seesaw”: Standard fish databases (Claverie & Wainwright 2014; Friedman et al. 2019) don’t trace the whole outline of the fish—they measure 17 dots on the skeleton, with 9 of those 17 dots (53%) packed inside the head and jaws and 0% on the outer dorsal, anal, or tail fins. context: It was also via our method—which deliberately includes the adversarial audit of advanced AI—that we were made aware of Thompson’s 1913 Herbert Spencer Lecture at Oxford, On Aristotle as a Biologist (Thompson 1913). The lecture makes the bold claim that Aristotle’s power as a philosopher comes from his strong localized knowledge and his initial concentration as a naturalist: the natural history of the lagoon at Pyrrha came first, and the metaphysics grew out of it. Thompson then goes further—the concept of the psyche (what we have since come to call the “soul”) is itself derived from the observation of nature. Aristotle’s De Anima classifies the soul the way he classified fishes: a nutritive soul shared with plants, a sentient and motile soul shared with animals, and a reasoning soul in man, each lower grade implicit in the higher “as a triangle within a square.” It is a nested geometry, not a ghost; and in De Anima II.4 that same psyche is named as the body’s formal, efficient, and final cause at once—the very analysis of causation that made Aristotle’s precise and elaborate taxonomies possible, and that still underlies many of our maps of nature. In that sense, if we want to understand what animates us, we may need to start not with the later, transmuted, and oversimplified idea of the soul, but with the original one: a graded, nested form, read off living bodies by a man who had spent his years dissecting cuttlefish on Lesbos.
